In the Greek New Testament, it is used in references to the Jewish Festival of Unleavened Bread and the food associated with it. The word appears nine times across nine verses, including passages in Matthew, Mark, Luke, Acts, and 1 Corinthians. Its basic meaning remains consistent: something prepared without leaven. The surrounding verse determines whether it describes the festival, the bread, or the time connected with this practice.

In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 14 times, including passages that speak of thorns among growing plants and a crown made from thorns. Its basic meaning remains the same wherever it appears, while the surrounding verse determines how the image or object functions in that passage.

d: Of another nation, a foreigner.
me: Adjective, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means “foreign”: it describes someone who comes from another people or place rather than belonging to the community being discussed. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 17:18. Its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains clear: the person is viewed as foreign to the community or setting. The word therefore identifies a person by their lack of native or local belonging.

d: To sit up.

e.t: This word means “to sit up,” describing the act of rising from a lying or seated position into an upright posture. It is an action word focused on becoming upright, rather than on the reason for doing so or what happens afterward. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice: once in Luke and once in Acts. The surrounding verse provides the specific situation in which the action occurs.

The surrounding sentence determines whether the emphasis is on releasing, loosening, or departing.

e.t: Apollyon is a personal name used for a particular figure in the Greek New Testament. It is not presented here as a broad description, action, or quality; its lexical role is to identify someone by name. This word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Revelation 9:11. The name’s precise significance in that passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

Its central meaning remains the removal of a person from synagogue fellowship or membership.

The precise emphasis—ceremony, feast, or the occasion as a whole—depends on the surrounding sentence.

Its exact force in any verse depends on what the surrounding passage says about the thought being considered.

The precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in John 19:37 and Revelation 1:7. Its basic meaning remains direct and physical: something is pierced or penetrated. The precise force of the action in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself points plainly to piercing.

Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains resting on or relying upon something rather than standing independently.

e.t: This word means “glorious.” It is a describing word for something marked by glory, greatness, or splendor. Its sense is positive and elevated, drawing attention to a quality that stands out impressively. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 2:20. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the description of something glorious.

Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains the same: red.

Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains a person marked out as a zealot.

The surrounding context is needed to explain the passage’s full significance, but the word itself consistently identifies a veil or covering rather than an abstract idea.

The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Mark 5:5. In the New Testament, it refers to the proclaimed message itself rather than merely the act of speaking. It is used nine times in the Greek New Testament, including passages that connect preaching with announcing God’s message and making Christ known. The word therefore emphasizes a declared proclamation—something spoken openly for others to hear, understand, and receive.

The available wording identifies the person simply as Crescens, but the surrounding verse text is not provided here, so no further role or circumstance should be assigned to him from the name alone. Its meaning at the lexical level is therefore the person’s name, Crescens.

me: Noun, Nominative, Plural, Neuter

e.t: The word refers to a corpse or dead body—the physical remains of someone who has died. It is a concrete term, not a description of a person’s character or spiritual condition. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Hebrews 3:17. Since the surrounding verse text is not available here, the word’s precise force in that sentence depends on its context; its basic meaning remains a dead body.

d: A redeemer, liberator, deliverer.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means “deliverer” or “redeemer”: someone who rescues or releases another from trouble, danger, or bondage. It presents a person as the one who brings needed deliverance, rather than merely describing the act of rescue itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 7:35. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning is a person who delivers or redeems.

d: (Divine) majesty, greatness.
me: Noun, Genitive, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word means “majesty”: greatness, dignity, and splendor belonging to one who is exalted. It is used as a noun, pointing to majestic status rather than describing an action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times—twice in Hebrews and once in Jude—and each occurrence is rendered “Majesty.” The word is associated with the exalted glory of God and with the supreme position of Christ, though the precise emphasis in any verse comes from its surrounding passage.

d: (a) indeed, really, (b) yet, however, nevertheless.

e.t: This word means “but” or “yet.” It is used to connect a statement with a contrasting or qualifying thought, often signaling that something remains true despite what has just been said. As a conjunction or connective expression, it helps the reader follow a turn in the sentence rather than naming a person, object, or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times, including five occurrences in John. Its precise force in any sentence depends on the surrounding words.

d: A ship, vessel.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “ship,” referring to a large watercraft used for travel or transport. It is a noun, so it names the vessel itself rather than an action or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 27:41. Its basic meaning is straightforward, while the surrounding verse determines what happened to that ship in that particular scene.

In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Peter 3:8; the surrounding verse text is needed to explain how Peter applies it there.
